slides: I mentioned this in one of the first lessons, but I'll say it again, because this is the place for it.
Writing an essay has three stages. Planning, producing the text, and checking. That's proofreading and corrections.
When you're short on time, and thirty-five minutes to plan, write and check is short, these stages get squeezed. You'll feel it in your first timed essay.
The stage that gets hurt the most is proofreading. Next is planning, because planning takes time. And producing the text gets hurt the least. I mean, we basically know how to write.
Now, the people who make the test understand this. So raters are told to look at the essay as a first draft only, and to judge it that way.
So your essay doesn't have to be perfect. It's not compared to the most perfect essay possible. It's compared to a draft written in thirty-five minutes, with little or no proofreading.
So the conclusion is, proofreading is almost unnecessary. I won't say completely, because that's not true. You can still improve things, and it's worth doing. Just not with a lot of time.
Leave two to three minutes for it. No more.
And in two or three minutes, you really can't go over the whole essay and fix everything. So let's see how to do it well.
Mainly, I correct language. Less content.
Content is hard to fix at this point. 'This argument isn't good enough, let's swap it'? You really can't.

And basically, if I planned right in the skeleton, there should be almost no content corrections. The skeleton splits the writing. Content is finished in the planning, and the writing itself is language.
So the mistakes you can still catch are most likely language mistakes.
So what do I check?
Punctuation. Maybe I missed a full stop, or a comma. And no comma splices. That's two full sentences joined with just a comma.
Agreement. Singular and plural. Subject and verb. A pronoun that matches what it refers to.
Articles. That's a classic one for Hebrew speakers. 'Government should' becomes 'the government should'.
Missing words, especially 'not'. One missing 'not' turns your position upside down.
And if I used an example or a comparison in an argument paragraph, I make sure there's a sentence that ties it back to the topic. That's something you can add in ten or twenty seconds.
I check that there's no repetition or padding. Just a reminder, that's when I say the same idea again in different words.
For example, I notice that at the end of a paragraph, I have a sentence that says almost the same thing as before. So I just delete the whole sentence.
And you don't need to fight with the eraser. To delete a whole sentence, just draw a line through it. It's not the neatest, but that's fine. They know it's a draft.
Focus and cohesion. I skim the essay, and I look for a missing connector between sentences, or something like that.
Again, I can't fix the whole essay. It's a quick check. But while I'm skimming, maybe I find a spot where one connector closes the gap.
And choose it by the relationship. Cause, result, contrast. A connector shows a relationship... it can't create one.
So how do we make corrections?

First, we leave a blank line between paragraphs. We also indent the first line of each paragraph, so actually, we don't really need the blank line. But we add it anyway, so we have room for corrections.
Where we can, we erase and rewrite. You're allowed to use an eraser. Bring one that really erases, and test it. Not the one on the end of the pencil, that tears the page and smears the pencil marks.
You can also use that little mark for adding a word, the caret, and write the word above it. But make it clear, so the rater understands you added a word here.
And remember, the pages are scanned. Anything written outside the lines, including the margins, isn't read.
And while we're talking about clarity... an essay that's hard to read might hurt your score. If your handwriting is a problem, start practising now.
I talked about leaving two or three minutes at the end. But if you practise and see you're okay with time, there's another option.
Proofread while you write. Every time you finish a paragraph, stop for a second, read it, check it's fine, and move on.

So why does this work? Well, yes, there's a main thread that runs through the whole essay. But each paragraph has a very specific, clear job. Think of all our lessons. Here's the opening, here's argument paragraph one, here's the rebuttal. We checked each one on its own.
The advantage is, you can fix things with less mess. You can even add two sentences. The disadvantage is, you might run out of time if you spend too long. So practise it, and see if it works for you.
With only two or three minutes at the end, we might not go over the whole essay.
A lot of the time, it's even better to go straight to a paragraph that felt a bit off while you were writing. Usually you can feel which paragraph sat well, and which one didn't.
If you know you have a paragraph with a problem, go fix it. The rest of the essay is probably fine.
